alignment.note: Greek uses the conjunction καί + adjective δευτέρα ('and a second'); the Vulgate renders this with secundum...autem, employing the postpositive adversative particle autem to mark a mild contrast absent from Greek and Syriac. Syriac compresses the whole into the single relative-prefixed form ܘܕܬܪܝܢ ('and that-of-second'), a typical economy of the Peshitta.

Greek ὁμοία and Syriac ܕܕܡܐ stand without an explicit copula; the Vulgate supplies the verb est ('is') to complete the Latin clause simile est, since Latin tolerates the verbless predicate less readily than the Semitic and Greek idioms.
αὕτη / ܠܗ / illi — the demonstrative/pronoun referring to the first commandment; Syriac uses the dative pronoun ܠܗ ('to it'), Latin the dative illi, both governed by the verb of likening.
ἀγαπήσεις / ܕܬܚܒ / Diliges — the future-as-imperative 'you shall love.'

Greek expresses 'your neighbour' analytically with article, adverbial substantive and genitive pronoun (τὸν πλησίον σου), matched by Latin proximum tuum; Syriac compresses noun and possessive suffix into the single inflected form ܠܩܪܝܒܟ, a normal Semitic morphological synthesis.
σεαυτόν / ܢܦܫܟ / teipsum — 'yourself'; Syriac idiomatically uses ܢܦܫܟ ('your soul/self'), the standard reflexive construction with נֶפֶשׁ.

The Vulgate inserts an explicit colon (:) before the quoted commandment, supplying punctuation that frames the Old Testament citation (Lev 19:18); neither the Greek nor Syriac mark the quotation orthographically here.

Greek expresses the comparison with the bare genitive of comparison τούτων ('than these'), and Latin likewise with the genitive horum; Syriac uses the analytic comparative ܡܢ ܗܠܝܢ ('from these'), the standard Semitic periphrasis for the comparative degree.
ἐντολή / ܦܘܩܕܢܐ / mandatum — 'commandment'; Syriac word order places the noun earlier in the clause than the Greek and Latin, a stylistic rearrangement only.

Greek negates with οὐκ ἔστιν and Latin with non est ('there is not'); Syriac employs the single negative existential particle ܠܝܬ, which fuses negation and the verb 'to be' in one lexeme, a characteristic Aramaic construction.
